Review Date: Reviewed in the United States on December 27, 2024
Review Body: As a recently retired teacher of 33 yrs., everything I have been witness to from 1997 to present day has been captured on paper with statistics and data to prove. It is mind boggling to think these trends and detriments to our children, their parents & family, and our communities & nations are so powerful and we are helpless to correct them with team work. It is my sincere hope we can find some harmony but I think it unlikely because I also believe the selfish “me” society and loss of empathy and communal pride in our world has stifled any chance we may have. There is something called the 10% Rule teachers look at. It used to be 10% of each class had challenging students, whether from social or economic circumstances that would create kids unprepared to keep up with the 90%. Over time it has flipped into a 10% of each class of kids who are responsible, motivated, eager and willing to learn, as well as supported by their nurturing supportive parents who are great role models. That is scary! Apple iPhones are a HUGE piece of that, but there is also the break down of education administrators who are unwilling to support the very people/teachers trying to guide and teach kids. That creates another big problem. Parents who think hats and phones are more important than their kids learning, don’t attend conferences, could care less because they are busy and tired and would rather be tick-too-big than deal with anything that might be uncomfortable to address. So the majority of people who should have the best interest in the student are hurting and not helping, now add the phone issue and the future is BlEaK:(

Review Date: Reviewed in the United States on October 7, 2024
Review Body: I’m a teacher and parent of young children and agree with the major points made in this book: no screens, no social media. However, this book seemed to perpetuate a lot of societal gender stereotypes to prove a point. There was also a strange tangential chapter in religion in which I think the author was trying to compare phones to God, but was really evangelizing? Basically a sensationalized research paper.

Review Date: Reviewed in the United States on August 4, 2024
Review Body: Well, I don't know about you, but when I buy a hardcover book, I want a good quality copy to last. I was disappointed to open the box and discover a generic yellow hardcover of poor quality. The book cover design is printed on a separate piece of paper, not the cover itself, and you just know it will wear out quality within the first use.

Review Date: Reviewed in the United States on May 17, 2024
Review Body: As a middle school teacher this book armed me with the data I’ve been needing to make my case to have a true cell phone ban and not just one on paper that is enforced by some and not by others. I highly recommend this book to parents, teachers, and really anybody else that is concerned about what’s happening to today’s kids/young adults and what may only get worse as time goes on.

Review Date: Reviewed in the United States on March 29, 2024
Review Body: I bought this book on audio which is a great way to go, something that struck me as I was listening to it and I had only gotten to chapter 3 is that what he was saying absolutely made sense considering my observations as a preschool teacher for 12 years, when I first started at the preschools I noticed that the kids were more independent and that the administration and the people who were creating the curriculums( I don't believe in curriculums for preschool children by the way, let them learn and grow) but the tendency when I first started was let them color Outside the Lines let them use a different color than green for a frog if they want to let them play outside let them learn math by counting the pebbles in the playground, about 5 years into it the tendency change to make them sit at a desk and practice writing their name make them sit at a desk and learn that a rose has to be yellow or pink, correct them if they're doing it incorrectly take their paper away and throw it away and give them another one until they get it right. That's not how the great inventors of our time developed! The tendency toward robotic children has extended two generations since the last time I was at the preschool my preschoolers grew up and raised up a generation of cyborgs who grew up and are now raising a generation of complete robots. There's one commercial on the air right now that plays over and over again I believe it's called LoveSac or something but it's a couch that you can change around and it's easily clean because you can peel the cover off of it and it's really a nice unit I'm not saying that the sofa itself is not good because I would love to have something that I could turn into a ball pit for the kids to play in and something that you can rearrange any old time and that you can just throw the cover in the washer, it's a good concept, but the problem is the commercial! They're saying oh you need to discover that it's okay to change things up, it's okay to switch things around, it's okay to change your mind, since when did it become not okay to do all those things since when are there such rules that people have to be told that it's okay to be yourself? That's where the problem is, and I'm not saying that the manufacturers or the advertisers are trying to brainwash people I'm just saying that they picked up on something that has been going on for the past 25 to 30 years and they're capitalizing on it because it works-because that's the way this generation thinks. We have unfortunately changed human beings to people who think that they have to ask permission if they need to blow their nose and not only that but they have to ask how is the proper way to do it, and nine times out of 10 they will go online and watch some influencer to find out how to blow their own nose. People need to realize that that's how dictators come into power and that's how people become oppressed
